edges.description: Swallowing faecally contaminated water delivers Vibrio cholerae to the small intestine, where the surviving inoculum uses the toxin-coregulated pilus to cross mucus and form microcolonies. The intermediates are known: gastric passage, then adherence.

Sanitation is not itself a route. Absent safe water and excreta disposal, faecally contaminated water becomes available to drink, so poor sanitation raises the chance of the ingestion route occurring rather than being that route.

nodes.description: Cholera toxin B subunit (CTB) binds to GM1 ganglioside and alternative fucosylated glycan receptors (e.g., Lewis X) on the apical surface of intestinal epithelial cells, initiating receptor-mediated endocytosis and retrograde trafficking to the endoplasmic reticulum.

V. cholerae uses the toxin-coregulated pilus (TCP) to traverse the intestinal mucus barrier, adhere to epithelial cells, and form microcolonies. TCP expression is controlled by the ToxR/TcpP/ToxT regulatory cascade. Biofilm formation enhances bacterial survival and transmission.
